en: The Sūtra on the Eighteen Nirayas Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty. The Buddha said:
"In the life of a human being, the days one sees the sun are few, while the days one does not see the sun are many. The transformations of good and evil do not [correspond]..."
Those who insult their parents or offend the Son of Heaven shall die and enter the *niraya* hells; these vary in depth and severity. There are eight hot *nirayas* and ten cold *nirayas*.
Those who fall below the midpoint of the earth enter the fire hells; those at the boundary between heaven and earth enter the cold hells.
If one has committed evil in the past but later performs good deeds, they will not enter the hells.

Those who kill people, steal from others, violate the wives of others, desire to cause death so as to obtain their wealth, who are defiled and treacherous, who delight in doing what is unwholesome, who scold and revile others, who flog, whip, or imprison them, who take pleasure in exposing the faults of others, who speak with jealousy and anger, who provoke the outbursts of wrath in others, and who act in opposition to heaven, earth, and the spirits—such individuals utterly lose their longevity and die to descend into the evil hells.

Later, they further transformed into goodness; there were those who did not enter the hells, for they knew that the Buddha-way undergoes transformation, and even if one enters the hells, one will certainly ascend to heaven.
Those who are fundamentally good ascend to *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is said that the Way of the Buddha must not be left unknown.

If base persons do not transform toward goodness, they enter the *niraya* hells where there is no joy; having entered the *niraya* hells, they become even more unwholesome, and their descent into the *niraya* hells becomes ever deeper.
Among those of this class, some may attain human birth; though they may be stern and evil, if they do not kill and instead love life, they will be swift in their movements as humans.
Those who abstain from eating meat will become even more swift;
if they possess hidden virtues, they will increase both their longevity and their swiftness.
"The first plow is named *Xianjiuhu* (First-Attaining-Existence), which in the human language means 'Arising Without Death.

When people dwell within this plow-field, they desire to fight upon seeing one another; though there are no weapons in the field, weapons appear spontaneously, and they wound and kill each other for countless years yet do not die."
Someone comes and tells them they will not die, and as soon as the wind blows upon them, they are healed.

This continues for countless years; then they are again struck and killed with glowing iron swords, then again killed with iron mallets, and wounded by extremely sharp fists; this is their lot for a long time, through countless years.

Those beings are tall and large; three thousand seven hundred and fifty years of human life constitutes one day for them, thirty such days constitute one month, and twelve such months constitute one year. Ten thousand years of their lifespan equals one hundred and thirty-five billion years of human life.
"The second plow is named *Kilotsila*; one *kilotsila* of suffering is equivalent to twenty [previous units].
It is like what people call 'binding them with ropes and fighting them.'"
Those people who dwell in this field are placed within a great fire; when they emerge red-hot, they are made to fight. They are then placed back into the fire;

when they emerge red-hot again, they are made to fight for several rounds. This continues for countless years. They are burned again, and upon emerging, they are made to fight, as if they could not die even while being subjected to such circularity. Thus they are reborn for countless years, and having done so, they run back into the fire again for countless years—such is their lot.

Those beings are tall and large; seven thousand five hundred years of human life constitutes one day for them, thirty such days constitute one month, and twelve such months constitute one year. Twenty thousand years of their lifespan is equivalent to two hundred seventy quadrillion years of human time.
“The third plow is named Saṃjīva (Reviving). One unit of suffering on Saṃjīva is equivalent to twenty units of Jālasaṃvartanīya (the Net-like), yet people call it ‘beating to death.

Those who dwell upon this plow are placed in fire whose heat is beyond description; looking left and right, they see mountains that appear like a place of pleasure. They run toward them and enter between them, but the mountains come together to crush them; yet they do not die, remaining there for countless years.”
Having been placed back into the fire, he was repeatedly cast out while glowing red, for countless years.

That person became tall and large; his lifespan was fifteen thousand years of the human world for one day, thirty such days for one month, and twelve such months for one year, with a total lifespan of forty thousand years, which corresponds to five hundred and forty billion years of the human world.
"The fourth plow is named Lou; one 'Lou' of suffering is equivalent to twenty 'Cheng-ju-du'. Yet people call it pleasure.

People dwelling on this plow live in a very large city, within which there are further smaller cities. Those who see them from the outside perceive that the interior is entirely filled with layered heavens. All those who enter therein become as red as molten iron."

Furthermore, within the inner city, the intense heat is beyond description; their flesh and skin are completely scorched, and for countless years they find neither rest nor sleep. Their flesh and bones are entirely consumed by fire, yet they are reborn again for countless years—such is their lot.

Those beings are tall and large; thirty days constitute a month, and twelve months constitute a year. Their lifespan is eighty thousand years, which corresponds to one thousand eight hundred billion years by human reckoning.
“The fifth plow is named Pangzuo (Side-Ending). One suffering on the Pangzuo is equal to twenty sufferings on the Lou (Roasting) plow, yet people call it ‘boiling until rotten.

Those who dwell upon this plow are cast into a vast, deep pit filled with fire; the guardians of the plow beat them with iron staves and thrust them inside, burning their bodies until they are completely charred, yet they do not die for countless years.”

Though they are burned by the accumulated fires, they do not die; yet they embrace fire and cling to human bodies, dying only to emerge from one cauldron and enter another, repeating this countless times—such is their lot.

Those beings are tall and large; sixty thousand human years constitute one day for them, thirty such days constitute one month, and twelve such months constitute one year. Their lifespan is one hundred and sixty thousand years, which corresponds to two trillion one hundred and sixty billion human years.
"The sixth plow is named Cao-wu-bei-ci; one suffering at Cao-wu-bei-ci is equivalent to twenty people at Pang-zu, yet people call it merely 'boiling heat'."
Those who dwell here find themselves within a city two thousand *li* high and four thousand *li* wide, filled with fire.

They are placed therein and covered over with iron for countless years; thus they find no rest, and it is said that for countless years they cannot lie down. Having been scorched, they are scorched again—such is their lot.

The beings there are tall and large; twelve thousand years among humans constitutes one day for them, thirty such days constitute one month, and twelve such months constitute one year. Their lifespan is three hundred and twenty thousand years, which corresponds to four trillion three hundred and twenty billion years among humans.
"The seventh plow is named Dūyanācca; in Dūyanācca there is one suffering, namely twenty times that of the *cāpāla* [hell], which people call being scorched and roasted by insects."
Those who dwell within this plow-field are like people impaled upon great iron spikes amidst a vast mass of fire; they remain there for countless years.
At times, a single gate opens and all the people rush toward it, desiring to exit;
yet the gate closes again, and they fall back into the fire for countless years.
Again, they see another gate open, and everyone runs toward it seeking to escape;
yet once they have exited the gate, they fall once more into a mire.
Within that mire are worms that gnaw at them, so that for countless years they cannot emerge—such is their lot.

Those beings are tall and large; twenty-four thousand years of the human world constitute one day for them, thirty such days constitute one month, and twelve such months constitute one year. Their lifespan is six hundred and forty thousand years, which corresponds to eight hundred and sixty-four billion years of the human world.
"The eighth plow is named Buludubanhu; one Buludubanhu of suffering is equivalent to twenty Duniannqie, as people say, 'the great suffering has ripened.'"

Dwelling within this plowshare, the ground is entirely ablaze; the executioners shall stand amidst the flames, roasting and skewering them. They are forced to remain upon their beds, unable to move and unable to rest, as they are scorched and singed.
Having been reborn there again, they remain for countless years; their suffering is ten thousand times greater than that of the plow-drawing hells, an agony beyond description—such is their lot.

These beings are tall and massive; forty-eight hundred thousand human years constitute a single day for them. Thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year. Their lifespan is one million two hundred and eighty thousand years, which corresponds to seventeen trillion two hundred and eighty billion human years.
The Buddha said:
"The fire plow is of eight kinds; when evil is great, it is deep and slow, but when evil is slight, it is shallow and easy.
'Plowing' is like a person confined in a prison as a prisoner, whose retribution is met in a distant place, dying in the wilderness while his family remains halfway along the road."

If one falls into this water and is born there, one cannot attain the Way until death. Upon entering the plow-field, there is suffering that is beyond description; it takes a long time before one can emerge. What is called the Cold Plow-field lies at the edge of the heavens.

There is a great mountain two thousand *li* high, whose primary function is to block the wind; it is named Mount Yúnquèlú. It is so dark that the sun and moon do not reach it. It is dark because of the obstructing great mountain, yet outside it, within the midst of the countless Cold Plow-fields, there are many kings of the sun and moon.
"The ninth plow is named Wu jing dou; one suffering of Wu jing dou is equivalent to twenty Bu lu dou ban hu, which in human language means 'to rise up violently.'"
People dwell upon this plowshare; the cold is beyond description. For countless years their bodies are completely frozen, yet they are repeatedly exposed to the elements, and twenty remain there.

Within the fire there is a sound; having already been subjected to it again, their limbs are broken as if by the discharge of a crossbow, and their severed parts are joined back together. Great stones are used to strike great infants; the pain is beyond description.
Having died there, they do not perish; rather, they are ground like iron millstones.
Having been ground thus, their feet are then ground, continuing until the entire body has been ground.
This continues for incalculable years, and the suffering is beyond description.

That person is tall and large; his lifespan is such that if one were to remove a single mustard seed every hundred years from a hundred twenty-eight hu of mustard seeds, by the time the seeds are exhausted, his life would not yet have ended. Such a person cannot even represent one ten-thousandth part of this [lifespan]. This is its kind.

Those who know the Buddha-way emerge quickly from suffering. If a person commits evil by day but refrains from transgression at night, they enter the plow [of rebirth] by day; yet if one commits evil at night while being free from transgression by day, their lack of peace at night is beyond description. Therefore, one must not fail to hear and know the Buddha-way.
"The tenth plow is named Nirarbu; one Nirarbu kalpa is equivalent to twenty Utkala-kalpas. The inhabitants there are tall and large;

their lifespan is such that if one were to remove a single mustard seed every hundred years from a heap of two hundred and fifty-six hu of mustard seeds, the seeds would be exhausted before their lifespan would end."
"The eleventh plow is named *Ulla*. One *Ulla* of suffering is equivalent to twenty *Nirarbuda*s.

Those people are tall and large; their lifespan is such that if one were to remove a single mustard seed every hundred years from five hundred and twelve *hu* of mustard seeds, by the time the seeds were exhausted, their life would not yet have ended."
"The twelfth plow is named Umman; one suffering of Umman is equivalent to twenty [sufferings] of Ulla.

Those people are tall and large, and their lifespan is one thousand twenty-four hu of mustard seeds; if one were to remove a single seed every hundred years, the seeds would be exhausted before their lifespan has ended."
"The thirteenth plow is named Wujie (Black-Thread). One suffering of Wujie is equivalent to twenty [sufferings] of Wuman (Black-Filled).

That person is tall and large; their lifespan is twenty-four thousand eight hundred bushels of mustard seeds. If one were to remove a single seed every hundred years, the mustard seeds would be exhausted before their lifespan had ended."
"The fourteenth plow is named Uhu. One Uhu of suffering is equivalent to twenty Ujjas.

Those people are tall and large; their lifespan is forty-nine thousand six hundred bushels of mustard seeds. If one were to remove a single seed every hundred years, the lifespan would not yet be exhausted when the mustard seeds were all gone."
"The fifteenth plow is named Sujānu; one suffering of Sujānu is equivalent to twenty *ūhas*.

That person is tall and large, and his lifespan is eight thousand one hundred and ninety-two *hu* of mustard seeds; if one were to remove a single seed every hundred years, the mustard seeds would be exhausted before his life has ended."
"The sixteenth plowing is named Mātuluṅgadhūpa. One suffering in Mātuluṅgadhūpa is equivalent to twenty Keṇa juices.

That person is tall and large; their lifespan is twelve thousand three hundred and eighty-four *hu* of mustard seeds. If one were to remove a single seed every hundred years, the mustard seeds would be exhausted before their life span has ended."
"The seventeenth plow is named Kūpuda. One *kūpuda* of suffering is equivalent to twenty *mātuluṅga* [dry] hells. The inhabitants there are tall and large;

their lifespan is thirty-two thousand seven hundred and sixty-eight *hu* of mustard seeds. If one were to remove a single seed every hundred years, the mustard seeds would be exhausted before their lifespan would end."
"The eighteenth plow is named Chenmo (Submergence). One instance of suffering in Chenmo is equivalent to twenty instances of Qubutu. The person there is tall and large;

their lifespan is sixty-five thousand five hundred and thirty-six *hu* of mustard seeds. If one were to remove a single seed every hundred years, the lifespan would not end until all the mustard seeds were exhausted. It is intensely cold and painful, beyond description and beyond words; it is ten thousand times greater than the suffering of other plows, such that the pain knows no limit."
The Buddha said:
"Regarding the eighteen hells, the matters for which people commit offenses—whether good or evil, light or heavy—are recorded in the *Niraya Sūtra*.
The Buddha said:

“There are eighteen hells, from the Great Phoenix and Dragon Hells down to the Hell of Small Insects; these constitute the eighteen hells in total. If a person performs much good and little evil, they will emerge from hell quickly; if they perform much evil and little good, they will emerge from hell slowly.”
The Buddha said:
"How could this place be guarded by ghosts? It is the dwelling of the eighteen hells, which are dark and gloomy.
Yet, when the Buddha was first born, from the heavens above to the heavens below, reaching as far as the thirty-two heavens, all eighteen hells were filled with light."

When the Buddha first attained the Way, there was another illumination; when the Buddha addressed the Brahma Heaven, there was another illumination; when the Buddha first practiced the Way and taught all under heaven, there was another illumination; and on the day of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was another illumination. These lights extended upward as far as the thirty-two heavens, so that it may be known that the Buddha-way must not remain unknown: those who do much good ascend to heaven, while those who do much evil enter the niraya.

If one is born as an animal, knowing the Buddha-way leads to immortality, that small person will surely attain long life; yet, though they frequently hear of the Buddha-way, they do not study it, do not draw near to virtuous people, and do not hear of wholesome deeds, and thus they shall remain subject to suffering and affliction.
Those who mock the Buddha-way fall deeply into the hells; for this reason, the Buddha censures them.

When people commit evil, they delight in reviling and foul speech, continuing until old age without ceasing. The heavenly deities loathe such persons and cause them to become birds, beasts, domestic animals, blood-spirited creatures, or insects; their descendants, in turn, serve as slaves to their former masters.
The Buddha said:

"If a person does not perform good deeds, they depart from the human realm to become insects or beasts; if born into a high household, they may become a ghost. How, then, could such a one obtain food from ghosts?"
The Buddha said:
"When a person performs good deeds, they ascend to the heavens; subsequently, they are reborn again in human form.
This concludes the *Buddha-sūtra on the Eighteen Nirayas*.
